The observations of objectionable conditions and practices listed on the front of this form
are reported:
1. Pursuant to Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, or
2. To assist firms inspected in complying with the Acts and regulations enforced by the
Food and Drug Administration.


Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

of a

laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or employee

The observations of objectionable conditions and practices listed on the front of this form
are reported:
1.
Pursuant to Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, or
2.
To assist firms inspected in complying with the Acts and regulations enforced by the
Food and Drug Administration.
Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and
prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

are reported:

Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

The observations of objectionable conditions and practices listed on the front of this form
are reported:
1. Pursuant to Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, or
2. To assist firms inspected in complying with the Acts and regulations enforced by the
Food and Drug Administration.


Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

are reported:
1. Pursuant to Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, or
2. To assist firms inspected in complying with the Acts and regulations enforced by the

Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

The observations of objectionable conditions and practices listed on the front of this form
are reported:
1. Pursuant to Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, or
2. To assist firms inspected in complying with the Acts and regulations enforced by the
Food and Drug Administration.


Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has been
prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

The observations of objectionable conditions and practices listed on the front of this form
are reported:
1. Pursuant to Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, or
2. To assist firms inspected in complying with the Acts and regulations enforced by the
Food and Drug Administration.


Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

The observations of objectionable conditions and practices listed on the front of this form
are reported:
1. Pursuant to Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, or
2. To assist firms inspected in complying with the Acts and regulations enforced by the
Food and Drug Administration.


Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

The observations of objectionable conditions and practices listed on the front of this form
are reported:
1. Pursuant to Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, or
2. To assist firms inspected in complying with the Acts and regulations enforced by the
Food and Drug Administration.


Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

Pursuant to Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, or
2.
To assist firms inspected in complying with the Acts and regulations enforced by the
Food and Drug Administration.
Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

The observations of objectionable conditions and practices listed on the front of this form
are reported:
1. Pursuant to Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, or
2. To assist firms inspected in complying with the Acts and regulations enforced by the
Food and Drug Administration.


Section 704(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 USC 374(b)) provides:
"Upon completion of any such inspection of a factory, warehouse, consulting
laboratory, or other establishment, and prior to leaving the premises, the officer or
employee making the inspection shall give to the owner, operator, or agent in charge a
report in writing setting forth any conditions or practices observed by him which, in his
judgment, indicate that any food, drug, device, or cosmetic in such establishment (1)
consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance, or (2) has
been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have become
contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health. A copy
of such report shall be sent promptly to the Secretary."

deep_analysis_input.body_full: FDA Review Violations were identified and documented during review of your drug manufacturing facility, Shenzhen Benliju Biotech Co., Ltd., FDA Establishment Identifier (FEI) 3013504845. This review was conducted under FDA’s statutory authority and public health responsibilities to protect the public from unsafe, ineffective, and poor quality drugs. Your facility is registered with the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a manufacturer of over-the-counter (OTC) drug products. FDA has reviewed the records you submitted in response to our January 20, 2026 request and subsequent correspondence, for records and other information pursuant to section 704(a)(4) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) for your facility. This warning letter summarizes significant violations of Current Good Manufacturing Practice (CGMP) regulations for finished pharmaceuticals. See Title 21 Code of Federal Regulations, parts 210 and 211 (21 CFR, parts 210 and 211). Because your methods, facilities, or controls for manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding of drugs as described in your response to our 704(a)(4) request do not conform to CGMP, your drug products are adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B)). Violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act The following are violations identified during our review. As a reminder, this is not an all-inclusive list of violations at your facility. 1. Your firm failed to have, for each batch of drug product, appropriate laboratory determination of satisfactory conformance to final specifications for the drug product, including the identity and strength of each active ingredient, prior to release. Your firm also failed to conduct appropriate laboratory testing, as necessary, for each batch of drug product required to be free of objectionable microorganisms (21 CFR 211.165(a) and 211.165(b)). Your firm manufactures OTC drug products such as (b)(4) which are labeled as “sterile.” Based on the records and information provided, you do not demonstrate that you conduct adequate finished drug product testing including microbiological tests on your OTC drug products. For example, you indicate that you do not test each batch of finished drug product for conformance to product release specifications before each batch release. This includes not conducting sterility testing on your drug product purporting to be sterile. Testing is an essential part of CGMP to ensure that the drug products you manufacture conform to all pre-determined quality attributes appropriate for their intended use. Drug products must be tested for identity and strength of the active ingredient, prior to release and distribution. Without adequate testing, you do not have scientific evidence to assure that your drug products conform to appropriate specifications before release. 2. Your firm failed to establish written procedures for production and process control designed to assure that the drug products you manufacture have the identity, strength, quality, and purity they purport or are represented to possess (21 CFR 211.100(a)). Based on the records and information you provided, you do not demonstrate that your manufacturing processes are reproducible and controlled to yield a product of uniform character and quality. Specifically, your response states that your firm does not have process validation procedures or process validation studies. This includes not conducting studies to demonstrate your process can ensure sterility of a drug product purporting to be sterile. Process validation evaluates the soundness of design and state of control of a process throughout its lifecycle. Each significant stage of a manufacturing process must be designed appropriately and assure the quality of raw material inputs, in-process materials, and finished drugs. Process qualification studies include intensive monitoring and testing throughout each significant process stage to characterize intra-batch variation and evaluate batches to determine whether an initial state of control has been established. Successful process qualification studies are necessary before commercial distribution. Thereafter, ongoing vigilant oversight of process performance and product quality is necessary to ensure you maintain a stable manufacturing operation throughout the product lifecycle. See FDA’s guidance document Process Validation: General Principles and Practices for general principles and approaches that FDA considers appropriate elements of process validation, at https://www.fda.gov/media/71021/download. 3. Your firm’s quality unit failed to exercise its responsibility to ensure drug products manufactured are in compliance with CGMP and meet established specifications for identity, strength, quality, and purity (21 CFR 211.22). Based on the records and information you provided, you do not demonstrate that your quality unit (QU) has adequately exercised its responsibilities and authority for the manufacture of your OTC drug products. For example, your QU failed to ensure the following: Adequate laboratory control procedures to ensure that drug products conform to appropriate standards of identity, strength, quality and purity (21 CFR 211.160(b)). The establishment of an adequate ongoing stability program (21 CFR 211.166(a)). Your firm’s quality systems are inadequate. For help implementing quality systems and risk management approaches to meet the requirements of CGMP regulations 21 CFR, parts 210 and 211, see FDA’s guidance documents Quality Systems Approach to Pharmaceutical CGMP Regulations at https://www.fda.gov/media/71023/download. Drug Recall On October 21, 2026, FDA held a teleconference with you, recommending that you recall all lots of (b)(4) you manufactured, within expiry, which are labeled as “sterile” as you have not demonstrated that these products are in fact sterile. On October 22, 2026, you agreed to the recall. CGMP Consultant Recommended Based upon the nature of the violations we identified at your firm, you should engage a consultant qualified as set forth in 21 CFR 211.34 to evaluate your operations and to assist your firm in meeting CGMP requirements. The qualified consultant should also perform a comprehensive six-system audit of your entire operation for CGMP compliance and evaluate the completion and efficacy of your corrective actions and preventive actions before you pursue resolution of your firm’s compliance status with FDA. Your use of a consultant does not relieve your firm’s obligation to comply with CGMP. Your firm’s executive management remains responsible for resolving all deficiencies and systemic flaws to ensure ongoing CGMP compliance. Conclusion As previously stated, you are responsible for investigating and determining the root causes of any violations and implementing corrective and preventative measures to ensure future and sustained compliance so that these violations and any others do not occur. FDA placed all drugs and drug products offered for import into the United States from your firm on Import Alert 66-40 on September 30, 2026. FDA may withhold approval of new applications or supplements listing your firm as a drug manufacturer until any violations are completely addressed and we confirm your compliance with CGMP. We may inspect to verify that you have completed corrective actions to any violations. Failure to address any violations may also result in the FDA continuing to refuse admission of articles manufactured at Shenzhen Benliju Biotech Co., Ltd., at Factory Building 303, Qihong Pinshun Industrial Park, 105 Pinshun Road, Guixiang Community, Guanlan Street, Shenzhen, Guangdong 518000, China into the United States under section 801(a)(3) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 381(a)(3). Articles under this authority that appear to be adulterated may be detained or refused admission, in that the methods and controls used in their manufacture do not appear to conform to CGMP within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B). Send your written response to CDER-OC-OMQ-Communications@fda.hhs.gov within fifteen (15) business days of receipt of this letter. If you have information that you believe demonstrates that your products are not in violation of the FD&C Act and FDA regulations, include that information for our consideration. Identify your written response with FEI 3013504845 and ATTN: Rory Geyer in the subject line of the email. FDA posts warning letters to www.FDA.gov. Sincerely, /S/ Francis Godwin Director Office of Manufacturing Quality Office of Compliance Center for Drug Evaluation and Research U.S. Food and Drug Administration cc: Registered U.S. Agent Pragmatic Compliance Inc. deep_analysis_input.body_full: FDA Inspection Deviations were observed and documented during an inspection of your drug manufacturing facility, Umicore Argentina S.A., FDA Establishment Identifier (FEI) 3009867894, at Calle 14 No. 229 Parque Industrial Pilar, Lote 13, Pilar, Buenos Aires, from June 4 to 9, 2026. This inspection was conducted under FDA’s statutory authority and public health responsibilities to protect the public from unsafe, ineffective, and poor quality drugs. This warning letter summarizes significant deviations from Current Good Manufacturing Practice (CGMP) for active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs). Because your methods, facilities, or controls for manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding do not conform to CGMP, your APIs are adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act), 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B). We reviewed your June 30, 2026, response to our Form FDA 483 in detail and acknowledge receipt of your subsequent correspondence. Violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act The following are deviations identified during our inspection and review. As a reminder, this is not an all-inclusive list of deviations at your facility. 1. Failure to adequately investigate and document out-of-specification results and implement appropriate corrective actions. You manufacture APIs (e.g. (b)(4) ) intended for use in (b)(4) drug products. You failed to adequately investigate over 300 out-of-specification (OOS) results related to assay, related substances/impurities, microbiological monitoring, and water quality since 2021, of which more than 200 OOS results were invalidated. Our investigators conducted a review of 30 OOS investigation records and found a consistent pattern: when Phase I investigations found no conclusive laboratory error, Phase II investigations were either not conducted or improperly attributed the failing results to analyst or procedural error. The initial OOS results were then invalidated based solely on passing results after reanalysis. Analyst retraining was uniformly applied as a corrective action, even when Phase I investigations confirmed that laboratory errors were not the root cause of the OOS. Your overreliance on human error as a root cause, particularly when no specific laboratory error is identified, is deficient. OOS laboratory results must be fully investigated, including the initiation of Phase II manufacturing investigations when appropriate. Additionally, your investigations into API samples that exceeded the specification for total aerobic count did not include microbial identification. You acknowledged that you lack a process to investigate elevated microbial counts, including too numerous to count results obtained from the (b)(4) of (b)(4) water samples. The lack of colony characterization during microbial OOS investigations was previously cited in your 2018 inspection. Identification of organisms is a fundamental part of investigations into microbial excursions. Further, your firm failed to adequately investigate recurring complaints of foreign particulate matter in your (b)(4) batches. You determined that the potential root cause of the particulate matter was (b)(4) ; however, you did not perform analytical characterization to confirm your potential root cause. Additionally, you failed to evaluate all observed particle types ( (b)(4) ) in your (b)(4) batches. In your response, you acknowledge deficiencies in your investigations and commit to reevaluating the previously closed OOS and complaint investigations. You commit to performing a three-year retrospective OOS review, as well as to establish a microbial identification program. You also commit to determining whether your (b)(4) water test method needs to be revised. Your response is inadequate. It lacks sufficient details regarding the preliminary assessment of reopened investigations and fails to implement appropriate interim controls for API batches potentially affected by improperly invalidated results. Additionally, your risk assessment for distributed batches lacks evidence or data to support your conclusions. Your commitment to establishing a microbial identification program does not include criteria for when identification is required or interim controls during program development. Your response also lacks evidence that remediation measures have been implemented to ensure that suspected laboratory errors are scientifically justified and that manufacturing causes are thoroughly investigated when laboratory errors cannot be conclusively identified. Inadequate investigations can lead to unidentified root causes, ineffective corrective action and preventive action (CAPA), and recurring problems that compromise your ability to manufacture safe and effective APIs. In response to this letter, provide: An independent, retrospective review of all critical investigations (including each in-process, release, and stability test specification failure) for the last three years as of the date of this letter. Evaluate the adequacy of each investigation, including, but not limited to: o Determine whether a thorough review of production (e.g., batch manufacturing records, adequacy of the manufacturing steps, suitability of equipment/facilities, variability of raw materials, process capability, written procedures deviation history, complaint history, batch failure history) was conducted. o Assess sufficiency of review of related data and investigations to identify if there are potential systemic linkages. o Evaluate adequacy of scope, rigor, staff investigation competencies, subject matter expertise, scientific/analytical foundation, root cause determinations, and CAPA. o Summary of findings of the assessment, and associated detailed CAPA, for each of the above elements. An independent assessment and remediation plan for your CAPA program. Provide a report that evaluates whether the program includes effective root cause analysis, ensures CAPA effectiveness, analyzes investigations trends, improves the CAPA program when needed, implements final quality unit decisions, and is fully supported by executive management. A retrospective, independent review of all invalidated OOS (including in-process and release/stability testing) results for U.S. products, irrespective of whether the batch was ultimately distributed in the United States, for the last three years from the initial date of inspection, and a report summarizing the findings of the analysis, including the following for each OOS: o Determine whether the scientific justification and evidence relating to the laboratory incident and OOS result conclusively or inconclusively demonstrates causative laboratory error. o For investigations that conclusively establish laboratory root cause, provide rationale and ensure that all other laboratory methods vulnerable to the same or similar root cause are identified for remediation. o For all laboratory incident and OOS results found by the retrospective review to have an inconclusive or no root cause identified in the laboratory, include a thorough review of production (e.g., batch manufacturing records, adequacy of the manufacturing steps, suitability of equipment/facilities, variability of raw materials, process capability, deviation history, complaint history, batch failure history). Provide a summary of potential manufacturing root causes for each investigation, and any manufacturing operation improvements. A comprehensive review and remediation plan for your OOS result investigation systems. The CAPA should include but not be limited to addressing the following: o Quality unit oversight of laboratory investigations o Identification of adverse laboratory control trends o Resolution of causes of laboratory variation o Initiation of thorough investigations of potential manufacturing causes whenever a laboratory cause cannot be conclusively identified o Adequately scoping of each investigation and its CAPA o Revised OOS investigation procedures with these and other remediations For more information about handling failing, out-of-specification, out-of-trend, or other unexpected results and documentation of your investigations, see FDA’s guidance document Investigating Out-of-Specification (OOS) Test Results for Pharmaceutical Production at https://www.fda.gov/media/158416/download. While this guidance addresses chemistry laboratory analyses, many of its principles are also relevant to investigating out-of-specification microbiological results and out-of-trend results. A possible laboratory error is insufficient to close an investigation at Phase 1. Whenever an investigation lacks conclusive evidence of laboratory error, a thorough investigation of potential manufacturing causes must be performed. 2. Failure to properly maintain equipment, buildings, and facilities used in the manufacture of API in a clean condition. You also failed to clean equipment and utensils to prevent contamination or carry-over of a material that would alter the quality of the API beyond the official or other established specifications. You failed to adequately maintain your equipment and facility in a good state of repair. For example, our investigators observed the following: Peeling material on the product contact side of the (b)(4) on (b)(4) tank (b)(4) . Unidentified (b)(4) residues near the openings and (b)(4) , and (b)(4) residues near the (b)(4) , on (b)(4) tanks (b)(4) , despite (b)(4) tanks being documented as “clean”. Stagnant water filling the transfer line between (b)(4) tanks (b)(4) . A flying insect was observed at the bottom of the (b)(4) tank (b)(4) . A cracked and damaged ceiling above (b)(4) tank (b)(4) , with (b)(4) particulate debris resting on top of the (b)(4) tank directly below. These conditions pose a contamination risk as the tank is opened during manufacturing and cleaning operations. Live insects on and around equipment and floors where (b)(4) , and API packaging activities occur. (b)(4) stored (b)(4) and in bins containing standing water and (b)(4) particles. These parts are used for (b)(4) API (b)(4) steps. Notably, you acknowledged that (b)(4) are not routinely sanitized, and that (b)(4) is replaced (b)(4) . (b)(4) water samples collected directly from (b)(4) without (b)(4) or (b)(4) , which is not representative of actual use conditions. In your response, you state that the peeling material observed on (b)(4) tank (b)(4) was excess construction base material. You attribute the (b)(4) residues observed in (b)(4) tanks (b)(4) to (b)(4) carryover, the brown residues to joint adhesive, and the stagnant water in the transfer line to inadequate slope. As a corrective action, you commit to revising the applicable cleaning procedures and state that the (b)(4) tanks and the transfer line were taken out of service, recleaned, and inspected. You acknowledge the ceiling damage above (b)(4) tank (b)(4) , but conclude the contamination risk was low, citing adequate spatial separation between the ceiling and the tank lid and the absence of manufacturing operations. While you state that the contamination risk was low, the ceiling was repaired and the area was cleaned prior to resuming operations. Finally, you acknowledge pest control program deficiencies and commit to revising your procedure to include all ISO-classified manufacturing areas, sealing identified pest entry points, and establishing a formal pest sighting reporting system. Your response is inadequate. It lacks supporting analytical data, appropriate controls, and retrospective impact assessments for previously manufactured batches. Your conclusion that the peeling material on (b)(4) tank (b)(4) is excess base material relies solely on your installation qualification report and is unsupported by analytical identification. You also fail to evaluate or provide a retrospective impact assessment to determine whether this material may have contaminated previous drug product batches. While you acknowledge that the transfer line was not designed to drain properly, you fail to explain how this equipment was repeatedly approved and released as “clean.” You also do not address whether your cleaning validations remain valid or if the lack of proper drainage may have an impact on API quality. Additionally, you provide no microbiological characterization of the product contact surfaces of the (b)(4) water (b)(4) , nor did you assess the risk of biofilm formation on prior batches. Your revised standard operating procedure requires “periodic sanitization” without defining frequency, intervals, or acceptance criteria necessary for a controlled and validated program. Further, you did not identify the debris on top of (b)(4) tank (b)(4) . You also did not evaluate the risk of particulate ingress during manufacturing or cleaning operations when the tank lid was open, nor did you provide a retrospective product impact assessment. Although you outline procedural updates to your pest control program, you fail to provide a robust, scientifically supported risk assessment to justify the disposition of API batches manufactured in areas during the period of uncontrolled pest activity. Proper equipment cleaning and facility maintenance are critical to preventing microbial, particulate, and chemical contamination in injectable drug APIs. Your failure to address underlying equipment and facility maintenance issues is concerning, given the incidence of OOS results, complaints, and inadequate root-cause investigations at your facility. In response to this letter, provide: Your CAPA plan to implement routine, vigilant operations management oversight of facilities and equipment. This plan should incorporate oversight from a qualified independent consultant and ensure, among other things, prompt detection of equipment/facilities performance issues, effective execution of repairs, adherence to appropriate preventive maintenance schedules, timely technological upgrades to the equipment/facility infrastructure, and improved systems for ongoing management review. A comprehensive, independent retrospective assessment of your cleaning effectiveness to evaluate the scope of cross-contamination hazards. Include the identity of residues, other manufacturing equipment that may have been improperly cleaned, and an assessment of whether cross-contaminated products may have been released for distribution. The assessment should identify any inadequacies of cleaning procedures and practices, and encompass each piece of manufacturing equipment used to manufacture more than one product. A procedure for your water system monitoring that specifies routine microbial testing of water to ensure its acceptability for use in each batch of drug products produced by your firm. The current action/alert limits for total counts and objectionable organisms used for your (b)(4) water system. Ensure that the total count limits for your (b)(4) water are appropriately stringent in view of the intended use of each of the products produced by your firm. A procedure governing your program for ongoing control, maintenance, and monitoring that ensures the remediated system consistently produces water that meets (b)(4) specifications and appropriate microbial limits. CGMP Consultant Recommended Based upon the nature of the deviations we identified at your firm, you should engage a consultant qualified to evaluate your operations and to assist your firm in meeting CGMP requirements. The qualified consultant should also perform a comprehensive six-system audit 1 of your entire operation for CGMP compliance and evaluate the completion and efficacy of your corrective actions and preventive actions before you pursue resolution of your firm’s compliance status with FDA. Your use of a consultant does not relieve your firm’s obligation to comply with CGMP. Your firm’s executive management remains responsible for resolving all deficiencies and systemic flaws to ensure ongoing CGMP compliance. Conclusion You are responsible for investigating and determining the root causes of any deviations and implementing corrective and preventative measures to ensure future and sustained compliance so that these deviations and any others do not occur. FDA may withhold approval of new applications or supplements listing your firm as a manufacturer until any deviations are completely addressed and we confirm your compliance with CGMP. We may re-inspect to verify that you have completed corrective actions to any deviations. Failure to address any deviations may also result in the FDA refusing admission of articles manufactured at Umicore Argentina S.A. Buenos Aires into the United States under section 801(a)(3) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 381(a)(3). Articles under this authority that appear to be adulterated may be detained or refused admission, in that the methods and controls used in their manufacture do not appear to conform to CGMP within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act, 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B). If you are considering an action that is likely to lead to a disruption in the supply of drugs produced at your facility, FDA requests that you contact CDER’s Drug Shortages Staff immediately, at drugshortages@fda.hhs.gov, so that FDA can work with you on the most effective way to bring your operations into compliance with the law. Contacting the Drug Shortages Staff also allows you to meet any obligations you may have to report discontinuances or interruptions in your drug manufacture under 21 U.S.C. 356C(b). This also allows FDA to consider, as soon as possible, what actions, if any, may be needed to avoid shortages and protect the health of patients who depend on your products. Send your written response to CDER-OC-OMQ-Communications@fda.hhs.gov within fifteen (15) business days of receipt of this letter 2 . If you have information that you believe demonstrates that your products are not in violation of the FD&C Act and FDA regulations, include that information for our consideration. Identify your written response with FEI 3009867894 and ATTN: Jamie Dion in the subject line of the email. FDA posts warning letters to www.FDA.gov. ### [Warning Letter · FDA] LGM Pharma Solutions, LLC — **{{TITLE_ISSUE}}** {{W1}} `Evidence B` · `FDA Warning Letter` · `Signal High (T3)` · `CGMP`
**발행일**2026-11-17

**발행 부서/일자**Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) · 11/02/2026
**핵심 사실** `근거: 공식 인덱스 + 보조 출처` {{W5}} **시사점** {{W6}} **점검 사항** {{W7}} **출처** 📰 정보출처 [링크](https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/compliance-actions-and-activities/warning-letters) · 📎 공식원본 [링크](https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/warning-letters/lgm-pharma-solutions-llc-736085-11022026)

deep_analysis_input.body_full: Violations were observed and documented during an inspection of your drug manufacturing facility, LGM Pharma Solutions, LLC, FDA Establishment Identifier (FEI) 3017140477 at 17802 Gillette Ave., Irvine, CA, from May 11 to May 18, 2026. This inspection was conducted under FDA’s statutory authority and public health responsibilities to protect the public from unsafe, ineffective, and poor quality drugs. This warning letter summarizes significant violations of Current Good Manufacturing Practice (CGMP) regulations for finished pharmaceuticals. See Title 21 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), parts 210 and 211 (21 CFR parts 210 and 211). Because your methods, facilities, or controls for manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding do not conform to CGMP, your drug products are adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act), 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B). We reviewed your June 9, 2026, response to our Form FDA 483 in detail and acknowledge receipt of your subsequent correspondence. Violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act The following are violations identified during our inspection and review. As a reminder, this is not an all-inclusive list of violations at your facility. 1. Your firm failed to thoroughly investigate any unexplained discrepancy or failure of a batch or any of its components to meet any of its specifications, whether or not the batch has already been distributed (21 CFR 211.192). Your firm failed to adequately investigate out-of-specification (OOS) assay results obtained at multiple stability testing timepoints of both process validation and commercial batches for (b)(4) tablets. For example, you attributed OOS assay results of process validation batches to variability of both your analytical method and the incoming raw material, (b)(4) . Your investigations concluded that these OOS results had no impact on drug product quality because the process validation batches were not released for commercial distribution. However, your investigation of OOS assay results for commercial batches listed the same root causes that were identified for process validation batches. Despite knowing this information, you continued to release commercial batches after your process validation batches. You did not perform comprehensive investigations and extend the investigations to identify true root causes. Despite failing results, you did not implement appropriate and effective corrective actions and preventive actions (CAPA). In addition, you did not take appropriate market action at the time you obtained a confirmed (b)(4) OOS assay result from a retest of (b)(4) tablets. Your OOS investigation remained open without scientific justification, and you delayed acknowledging your drug product failure’s impact on drugs that remained in distribution. In your response, you state that inherent variability of the (b)(4) step of the analytical method may have contributed to OOS results. Your response is inadequate because you did not provide data to support your claim of method variability. Your method validation should account for any inherent variability in drug product testing. You are responsible for ensuring that your method is suitable for its intended use. In addition, you did not provide a risk assessment of the quality impact of the OOS results on several batches of (b)(4) tablets that you manufactured and remain in expiration in the U.S. market. Furthermore, your OOS investigations were not extended to include an evaluation of your manufacturing process. It is essential to conduct thorough well documented, and scientifically sound investigations to identify root causes of OOS results, evaluate all potentially affected batches, and implement timely and effective CAPA plans. Whenever an investigation lacks conclusive evidence of laboratory error, a thorough investigation of potential manufacturing causes must be performed. For more information about handling failing, out-of-specification, out-of-trend, or other unexpected results and documentation of your investigations, see FDA’s guidance document Investigating Out-of-Specification (OOS) Test Results for Pharmaceutical Production at https://www.fda.gov/media/158416/download. In response to this letter, provide: A comprehensive independent assessment of your laboratory practices, procedures, methods, equipment, documentation, and analyst competencies. Based on this review, provide a detailed plan to remediate and evaluate the effectiveness of your laboratory system. A retrospective, independent review of all invalidated OOS (including in-process and release/stability testing) results for drug products currently in the U.S. market and within expiry as of the date of this letter and a report summarizing the findings of the analysis, including the following for each OOS: o Determine whether the scientific justification and evidence relating to the invalidated OOS result conclusively or inconclusively demonstrates causative laboratory error. o For investigations that conclusively establish laboratory root cause, provide rationale and ensure that all other laboratory methods vulnerable to the same or similar root cause are identified for remediation. o For all OOS results found by the retrospective review to have an inconclusive or no root cause identified in the laboratory, include a thorough review of production (e.g., batch manufacturing records, adequacy of the manufacturing steps, suitability of equipment/facilities, variability of raw materials, process capability, deviation history, complaint history, batch failure history). Provide a summary of potential manufacturing root causes for each investigation and any manufacturing operation improvements. A comprehensive review and remediation plan for your OOS result investigation systems. The CAPA should include but not be limited to addressing the following: o Quality unit oversight of laboratory investigations o Identification of adverse laboratory control trends o Resolution of causes of laboratory variation o Initiation of thorough investigations of potential manufacturing causes whenever a laboratory cause cannot be conclusively identified o Adequate scoping of each investigation and its CAPA o Revised OOS investigation procedures with these and other remediations 2. Your firm failed to establish adequate written procedures for production and process control designed to assure that the drug products you manufacture have the identity, strength, quality, and purity they purport or are represented to possess (21 CFR 211.100(a)). Your firm failed to adequately validate the manufacturing processes for your (b)(4) tablets. Specifically, your process validation protocol required passing results for three batches of the (b)(4) . During process performance qualification (PPQ), (b)(4) batch of (b)(4) failed to meet (b)(4) specification for one of the active ingredients, (b)(4) . Your process validation report was approved despite the confirmed OOS (b)(4) failure which your report stated could not be adequately investigated because the remaining (b)(4) was consumed by tablet manufacturing. No justification or scientific rationale was included in your decision to conclude that your process validation was acceptable. You also did not adequately assess in-process critical quality attributes (CQA) for the (b)(4) and (b)(4) tablets. For example, your process validation report stated there was variability for both particle size distribution of the (b)(4) , and tablet thickness. In addition, your report stated that data results for these quality attributes were outside of your proposed ranges. You did not establish appropriate specifications for these attributes to ensure your finished drug products are manufactured reliably and reproducibly. Furthermore, several process validation batches of (b)(4) tablets were reported with OOS assay results for (b)(4) at various stability timepoints. You concluded that these failures had no drug product quality impact or risk to patients because they were not distributed to the U.S. market. These multiple OOS results, obtained during PPQ for your (b)(4) tablets, demonstrate a process that is not in a state of control. Appropriate controls and understanding of your manufacturing process are essential to ensuring a safe and effective drug product. We acknowledge that commercial batch (b)(4) of (b)(4) Tablets USP, (b)(4) ( (b)(4) mg) that you manufactured was recalled for being (b)(4) for (b)(4) . We acknowledge that you have discontinued the manufacture and distribution of (b)(4) drug products, including (b)(4) tablets. This drug product has a narrow therapeutic range, adherence to the established specification of the label claim for the active ingredients is critical; it is especially important to prevent patients with (b)(4) from receiving insufficient or excessive doses. In your response, you state that the majority of your investigations conclude the root cause for upward trending (b)(4) assay stability results for commercially distributed batches is likely due to the inherent variability of the (b)(4) step of the analytical method that you use. You also state that “…none of the commercial [batches] have a reportable result that lies outside the… specification[s] of the label [claim]….” You also indicate in your response that you could better understand the variability of your method and will evaluate and trend stability and release data for current batches. Your response is inadequate. You did not provide trended drug product release and stability data for the (b)(4) tablets that remain in expiration and on the U.S. market. In addition, you have not fully and adequately evaluated your manufacturing process which includes the analytical method and establishing appropriate specifications for in-process CQA. Your manufacturing process must be designed to consistently maintain a state of control so that it meets all of its chemical and microbiological attributes throughout its life cycle. Process validation evaluates the soundness of design and state of control of a process throughout its lifecycle. Each significant stage of a manufacturing process must be designed appropriately and assure the quality of raw material inputs, in-process materials, and finished drugs. Process qualification studies include intensive monitoring and testing throughout each significant process stage to characterize intra-batch and inter-batch variation and determine whether an initial state of control has been established. Successful process qualification studies are necessary before commercial distribution. Thereafter, ongoing vigilant oversight of process performance and drug product quality is necessary to ensure you maintain an ongoing state of control throughout the drug product lifecycle. See FDA’s guidance document Process Validation: General Principles and Practices for general principles and approaches that FDA considers appropriate elements of process validation at https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidancedocuments/process-validation-general-principles-and-practices. In response to this letter, provide: A remediation plan that better assures ongoing management oversight throughout the manufacturing lifecycle of all drug products. Provide a more data-driven and scientifically sound program that identifies sources of process variability, and assures that manufacturing operations meet appropriate parameters and quality standards. This includes, but is not limited to, evaluating suitability of equipment for its intended use, ensuring quality of input materials, determining the capability and reliability of each manufacturing process step and its controls, and vigilant ongoing monitoring of process performance and drug product quality. A detailed summary of your validation program approved at the time of manufacturing of this drug product to support the current batches that remain in expiration in the U.S. market. Also, include an assessment of your validation program for all other drug products that you manufactured and distributed to the U.S. market ensuring a state of control throughout the drug product lifecycle, along with associated procedures. Describe your program for process performance qualification, and ongoing vigilant monitoring of both intra-batch and inter-batch variation to ensure a continuing state of control. Also, describe your equipment and facility qualification program. A timeline for performing appropriate process performance qualification for each of your marketed drug products. Also provide a risk assessment and any follow up actions to be taken for the distributed drug products produced prior to performing any process validation studies. Drug Production Ceased We acknowledge your commitment to cease production of (b)(4) drug products at this facility. If you plan to resume any manufacturing operations for (b)(4) drug products, notify this office before resuming your drug manufacturing operations. If you resume CGMP activities, you are responsible for resolving all deficiencies and systemic flaws to ensure your firm is capable of ongoing CGMP compliance. In your notification to the Agency, provide a summary of your remediations to demonstrate that you have appropriately completed all CAPA. CGMP Consultant Recommended Based upon the nature of the violations we identified at your firm, you should engage a consultant qualified as set forth in 21 CFR 211.34 to assist your firm in meeting CGMP requirements. The qualified consultant should also perform a comprehensive six-system audit of your entire operation for CGMP compliance and evaluate the completion and efficacy of all corrective action and preventive action, before you pursue resolution of your firm’s compliance status with FDA. Your use of a consultant does not relieve your firm’s obligation to comply with CGMP. Your firm’s executive management remains responsible for resolving all deficiencies and systemic flaws to ensure ongoing CGMP compliance. Conclusion You are responsible for investigating and determining the root causes of any violations and implementing corrective and preventative measures to ensure future and sustained compliance so that these violations and any others do not occur. Unresolved violations may prevent other Federal agencies from awarding contracts. Failure to address violations may also cause FDA to withhold issuance of Export Certificates. FDA may withhold approval of new applications or supplements listing your firm as a drug manufacturer until any violations are completely addressed and we confirm your compliance with CGMP. We may re-inspect to verify that you have completed corrective actions to address any violations. If you are considering an action that is likely to lead to a disruption in the supply of drugs produced at your facility, FDA requests that you contact CDER’s Drug Shortages Staff immediately, at drugshortages@fda.hhs.gov, so that FDA can work with you on the most effective way to bring your operations into compliance with the law. Contacting the Drug Shortages Staff also allows you to meet any obligations you may have to report discontinuances or interruptions in your drug manufacture under 21 U.S.C. 356c(b). This also allows FDA to consider, as soon as possible, what actions, if any, may be needed to avoid shortages and protect the health of patients who depend on your drug products. Send your written response to CDER-OC-OMQ-Communications@fda.hhs.gov within fifteen (15) business days of receipt of this letter 1 . Identify your written response with FEI 3017140477 and ATTN: Christina Alemu-Cruickshank in the subject line of the email. If you have information that you believe demonstrates that your drug products are not in violation of the FD&C Act and FDA regulations, include that information for our consideration. FDA posts warning letters to www.FDA.gov. Sincerely, /S/ Francis Godwin Director Office of Manufacturing Quality Office of Compliance Center for Drug Evaluation and Research U.S. Food and Drug Administration ________________ 1 Under program enhancements for the Generic Drug User Fee Amendments (GDUFA) reauthorization for fiscal years (FYs) 2023-2027, also known as the GDUFA III Commitment Letter, your facility may be eligible for a Post-Warning Letter Meeting to obtain preliminary feedback from FDA on the adequacy and completeness of your corrective action plans Content current as of: 11/17/2026 Regulated Product(s) Drugs Feedback FDA Archive About FDA Accessibility Visitor Information Website Policies / Privacy No FEAR Act Vulnerability Disclosure Policy FOIA HHS.gov USA.gov Contact FDA Follow FDA on Facebook Follow FDA on X Follow FDA on Instagram Follow FDA on LinkedIn View FDA videos on YouTube Subscribe to FDA RSS feeds Contact Number 1-888-INFO-FDA (1-888-463-6332) Back to Top

**핵심 사실** `근거: 공식 인덱스 + 보조 출처` {{W5}} **시사점** {{W6}} **점검 사항** {{W7}} **출처** 📰 정보출처 [링크](https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/compliance-actions-and-activities/warning-letters) · 📎 공식원본 [링크](https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/warning-letters/natural-essentials-inc-738543-11102026)

deep_analysis_input.body_full: FDA Inspection Violations were observed and documented during an inspection of your drug manufacturing facility, Natural Essentials Inc., FDA Establishment Identifier (FEI) 1520307, at 10375 State Route 43, Streetsboro, from June 22 to 26, 2026. This inspection was conducted under FDA’s statutory authority and public health responsibilities to protect the public from unsafe, ineffective, and poor quality drugs. This warning letter summarizes significant violations of Current Good Manufacturing Practice (CGMP) regulations for finished pharmaceuticals. See Title 21 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), parts 210 and 211 (21 CFR parts 210 and 211). Because your methods, facilities, or controls for manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding do not conform to CGMP, your drug products are adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act), 21 U.S.C. 351(a)(2)(B). We reviewed your August 11, 2026, response to our Form FDA 483 in detail. Violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act The following are violations identified during our inspection and review. As a reminder, this is not an all-inclusive list of violations at your facility. 1. Your firm failed to thoroughly investigate any unexplained discrepancy or failure of a batch or any of its components to meet any of its specifications, whether or not the batch has already been distributed (21 CFR 211.192). You failed to adequately investigate multiple out-of-specification (OOS) and out-of-limit (OOL) results from your drug component and over-the-counter (OTC) drug product testing. For example: Your (b)(4) assay result for (b)(4) Lot (b)(4) drug product exceeded the (b)(4) % specification limit, and retesting confirmed the OOS result. Instead of rejecting the entire lot, you released most of the lot based on passing results obtained from additional limited sampling which did not ensure all drug products released met your (b)(4) assay specification. Your practice of rejecting a partial drug product batch is an indication that your firm does not have well-controlled manufacturing and release procedures. Between 2025 and 2026, you conducted several investigations into microbial growth detected during your drug product final release testing. You did not identify the recovered microorganisms. These investigations did not conclusively establish root cause(s) for the failing results. Nevertheless, you released the affected lots based on passing retest results, invalidating the original failing results without scientific justification. Between 2024 and 2026, you conducted multiple OOS and out-of-limit (OOL) investigations for (b)(4) samples that exceeded (b)(4) , and microorganism limits. These investigations did not consider whether your (b)(4) system was adequately validated to ensure it consistently produces (b)(4) meeting (b)(4) United States Pharmacopeia (USP) monograph specifications and appropriate microbial limits. FDA’s 2023 inspection noted incomplete validation of your (b)(4) system and inadequate investigations into microbial recoveries, including (b)(4) , in your (b)(4) samples. Passing retest results alone cannot serve as the basis for invalidating OOS results. As a manufacturer, you have a responsibility to fully investigate failing chemical and microbial test results that may impact drug product quality. In your response, you attribute the (b)(4) of (b)(4) in (b)(4) Lot (b)(4) to inadequate (b)(4) time. You revised your (b)(4) procedures and retrained personnel. You acknowledge that (b)(4) failures were not investigated. You initiated a retrospective (b)(4) excursion assessment, revised your investigation procedures to require documentation of (b)(4) investigations, and incorporated (b)(4) data into your (b)(4) system monitoring program. Additionally, you revised your OOS procedure to strengthen investigations requirements for laboratory testing errors and to require documented scientific justification and quality unit approval prior to invalidating any OOS result. Your response is inadequate. The scope and criteria of your retrospective batch review is undefined, and your sampling strategy remains scientifically unjustified. You lack a risk assessment for the more than (b)(4) units of (b)(4) Lot (b)(4) that were released despite the unresolved investigation conclusion. You do not establish the relationship between (b)(4) and (b)(4) time. Additionally, you lack a retrospective risk assessment of finished drug product lots released with inappropriately invalidated microbial test results. You do not describe how you plan to ensure that your laboratory investigations are robust and clearly identify potential sources of contamination. Further, you do not identify root cause(s) for the (b)(4) , and microbial contamination failures, nor do you provide details of your interim controls in place to ensure product quality while corrective actions and preventive actions (CAPA) are ongoing. It is essential to conduct thorough, well documented, and scientifically sound investigations to identify root causes of OOS results, evaluate all potentially affected batches, and implement timely and effective CAPA plans. Whenever an investigation lacks conclusive evidence of laboratory error, a thorough investigation of potential manufacturing causes must be performed. For more information about handling failing, OOS, or other unexpected results and documentation of your investigations, see FDA’s guidance document Investigating Out-of-Specification (OOS) Test Results for Pharmaceutical Production at https://www.fda.gov/media/158416/download. While this guidance addresses chemistry laboratory analyses, many of its principles are also relevant to investigating OOS microbiological results and OOT results. In response to this letter, provide: A retrospective, independent review of all invalidated OOS (including in-process and release/stability testing) results for U.S. products for the last three years from the initial date of inspection and a report summarizing the findings of the analysis, including the following for each OOS: o Determine whether the scientific justification and evidence relating to the invalidated OOS result conclusively or inconclusively demonstrates causative laboratory error. o For investigations that conclusively establish laboratory root cause, provide rationale and ensure that all other laboratory methods vulnerable to the same or similar root cause are identified for remediation. o For all OOS results found by the retrospective review to have an inconclusive or no root cause identified in the laboratory, include a thorough review of production (e.g., batch manufacturing records, adequacy of the manufacturing steps, suitability of equipment/facilities, variability of raw materials, process capability, deviation history, complaint history, batch failure history). Provide a summary of potential manufacturing and testing root causes for each investigation, and any manufacturing operation improvements. A comprehensive review and remediation plan for your OOS and OOL result investigation systems. The CAPA should include, but not be limited to, addressing the following: o Quality unit oversight of laboratory investigations o Identification of adverse laboratory control trends o Resolution of causes of laboratory variation o Initiation of thorough investigations of potential manufacturing causes whenever a laboratory cause cannot be conclusively identified o Adequate scoping of each investigation and its CAPA o Revised OOS investigation procedures with these and other remediations o A similar review and remediation of your system for handling OOL findings (i.e., data that falls outside action limits) A detailed risk assessment addressing the potential effects of the observed (b)(4) system failures on the quality of all drug product lots currently in U.S. distribution or within expiry. Specify actions that you will take in response to the risk assessment, such as customer notifications and product recalls. 2. Your firm failed to establish laboratory controls that include scientifically sound and appropriate specifications, standards, sampling plans, and test procedures designed to assure that components, drug product containers, closures, in-process materials, labeling, and drug products conform to appropriate standards of identity, strength, quality, and purity (21 CFR 211.160(b)). (b)(4) Specifications Your (b)(4) specification limit for (b)(4) (e.g. not more than (b)(4) parts per million) exceeded the (b)(4) USP monograph specification limit (e.g., not more than (b)(4) parts per million). The review of your (b)(4) OOS investigations conducted between 2024 and 2026 documented (b)(4) measurements as high as (b)(4) ppm. In your response, you acknowledge your internal (b)(4) specification deviated from the USP < (b)(4) > requirements and state that a third-party evaluation confirmed your (b)(4) system can meet the USP specification. You commit to revising your standard operating procedure to align acceptance criteria with USP < (b)(4) >, updating your validation, and revising (b)(4) investigation procedures. Your response is inadequate. You do not provide a risk assessment of drug products manufactured using (b)(4) that did not meet USP specifications. You also do not provide data demonstrating that your (b)(4) system is adequately validated to ensure your (b)(4) system will consistently produce (b)(4) that is appropriate for pharmaceutical use and meets the USP monograph for (b)(4) . Further, you do not describe any interim controls in place to ensure product quality while you revalidate your (b)(4) system. Microbial Test Methods You use the (b)(4) for microbiological testing of your finished drug products (e.g., total aerobic microbial count and total yeast and mold counts). You failed to demonstrate that this (b)(4) test method is equivalent to or better than USP compendial methods and suitable for its intended use. Additionally, you did not align your procedure’s incubation times and temperature specifications with USP <61> specifications. The (b)(4) microbiological testing methodology uses qualitative pass/fail criterion that does not ensure appropriate quantitative enumeration results. The method is inadequate because it does not provide sufficient data on contamination levels, which is essential for trend analysis and evidence-based risk assessment to support quality evaluations and patient safety. Further, this system does not meet the minimum requirements for adequate identification of specified and objectionable microorganisms. Consequently, you are unable to perform speciation of the microbial contaminants recovered from the affected finished drug product lots. Test methods must be validated to demonstrate they are suitable for their intended use, reproducible, equivalent or superior to applicable USP compendial methods, and capable of detecting the presence of objectionable microorganisms in each component or finished drug product. In response to this letter, provide: A comprehensive independent assessment of your laboratory practices, procedures, methods, equipment, documentation, and analyst competencies. Based on this review, provide a detailed plan to remediate and evaluate the effectiveness of your laboratory system. A comprehensive evaluation of microbiological tests methods used to perform total counts and identification to evaluate suitability for intended use, followed by systemic CAPA, including but not limited to: o A comprehensive retrospective evaluation review of each test method to determine any inadequacies, including but not limited to those cited in this letter. o Where a method is found unsuitable for its intended use (e.g., inadequate capacity to enumerate), provide information on a new suitable method that will be employed o Improved systems to ensure selection and suitability of microbiological test methods in future before implementation. o Once this full evaluation is complete, provide all findings, data, and deviations encountered. Following review by an independent third-party, provide updated validation protocols and final reports that adequately address methods for each product, including specificity, limit of detection, robustness, ruggedness, and repeatability. This should include an evaluation of whether sample sizes are appropriate. Where you intend to use non-compendial methods, provide studies evaluating the equivalence or superiority of the method to the USP method. Updated analytical procedures, including confirmatory testing and speciation, that ensure regulatory compliance for all microbiological testing. This should also include an explanation of whether sample preparations are reserved to assist in conducting OOS investigations. A thorough remediation plan to operate a suitable (b)(4) system. Include a robust ongoing control, maintenance, and monitoring program to ensure the remediated system consistently produces (b)(4) adhering to (b)(4) , USP, monograph specifications and appropriate microbial limits. 3. Your firm failed to conduct at least one test to verify the identity of each component of a drug product (21 CFR 211.84(d)(1)). You failed to perform adequate identity testing of each incoming lot of (b)(4) used as a component in the manufacture of your OTC (b)(4) drug products. For example, you failed to adequately test your incoming (b)(4) , used as an active ingredient, for (b)(4) . Identity testing of high-risk drug components, such as (b)(4) , includes limit tests in the USP to ensure that the component meets the relevant safety limits for (b)(4) levels. Because you did not perform identity testing on each shipment of each lot using the USP identification test that detects hazardous impurities, you failed to ensure the acceptability of these components for use in the manufacture of your drug products. In your response, you identify several drug products that contain (b)(4) and commit to testing reserve samples to confirm the absence of (b)(4) contamination. You also commit to working with a third-party laboratory to develop an in-house method to test for the presence of (b)(4) in (b)(4) . Your response is inadequate. You do not commit to implementing routine USP monograph identity testing requirements for (b)(4) , which includes a limit test for (b)(4) , nor do you provide test results for reserve samples of (b)(4) containing drug products. Furthermore, you do not evaluate other components used to manufacture your drug products for compliance with all applicable USP monograph identity requirements. The use of (b)(4) contaminated with (b)(4) has resulted in various lethal poisoning incidents in humans worldwide. See FDA’s guidance document (b)(4) In response to this letter, provide: The chemical and microbiological quality control specifications you use to test and release each incoming lot of components for use in manufacturing. A description of how you will test each component lot for conformity with all appropriate specifications for identity, strength, quality, and purity. Include a commitment to always conduct at least one specific identity test for each incoming component lot. In the case of (b)(4) , and certain additional high-risk components we note that this includes the performance of (b)(4) of the USP monograph. A commitment to provide (b)(4) test results, no later than 30 calendar days from the date of this letter, from testing retains for all lots of components within expiry of manufactured drug products. Alternatively, if a retain of a component lot is unavailable, perform retain sample testing of all implicated finished drug product batches for the presence of (b)(4) . 4. Your firm failed to ensure that laboratory records included complete data derived from all tests necessary to ensure compliance with established specifications and standards (21 CFR 211.194(a)). You failed to exercise appropriate controls over your computerized systems. During the inspection, you admitted to preserving raw chromatographic data but failing to retain the processed chromatograms. Additionally, you lacked adequate controls for the spreadsheets and documents used for CGMP data entry, review, and retention. During the inspection, our investigator identified several uncontrolled and unlocked worksheets containing CGMP trending data for the (b)(4) system, leaving the data vulnerable to alteration or deletion. In your response, you commit to developing an electronic records control procedure, restricting unauthorized modification of spreadsheets used for CGMP data processing, and initiating a retrospective data integrity assessment. You established interim measures, including independent analyst and quality unit review of processed chromatograms prior to disposition, and evaluating your chromatographic software for enhanced data retention and audit trail capability. Your response is inadequate. You do not explain how your retrospective assessment will comprehensively identify data integrity and control gaps. This is concerning because post-analysis modifications prevent the reconstruction of previously processed chromatograms. You also do not explain how you will validate your spreadsheets to ensure formulas are accurate and secure from manipulation. Additionally, you provide no timelines for finalizing procedures or completing your chromatography software evaluation and validation. In response to this letter, provide: A comprehensive assessment of documentation systems used throughout your manufacturing and laboratory operations to determine where documentation practices are insufficient. Include a detailed CAPA plan that comprehensively remediates your firm’s documentation practices to ensure you retain attributable, legible, complete, original, accurate, contemporaneous records throughout your operation. An updated validation for your chromatography peak processing method and evidence that the processed chromatograms are retained within the computer system. CGMP Consultant Recommended Based upon the nature of the violations we identified at your firm, you should engage a consultant qualified as set forth in 21 CFR 211.34 to evaluate your operations and to assist your firm in meeting CGMP requirements. The qualified consultant should also perform a comprehensive six-system audit 1 of your entire operation for CGMP compliance and evaluate the completion and efficacy of your corrective actions and preventive actions before you pursue resolution of your firm’s compliance status with FDA. Your use of a consultant does not relieve your firm’s obligation to comply with CGMP. Your firm’s executive management remains responsible for resolving all deficiencies and systemic flaws to ensure ongoing CGMP compliance. Conclusion You are responsible for investigating and determining the root causes of any violations and implementing corrective and preventative measures to ensure future and sustained compliance so that these violations and any others do not occur. Unresolved violations may prevent other Federal agencies from awarding contracts. Failure to address violations may also cause FDA to withhold issuance of Export Certificates. FDA may withhold approval of new applications or supplements listing your firm as a drug manufacturer until any violations are completely addressed and we confirm your compliance with CGMP. We may re-inspect to verify that you have completed corrective actions to address any violations. Send your written response to CDER-OC-OMQ-Communications@fda.hhs.gov within fifteen (15) business days of receipt of this letter. If you have information that you believe demonstrates that your products are not in violation of the FD&C Act and FDA regulations, include that information for our consideration. Identify your written response with FEI 1520307 and ATTN: Christopher Keating in the subject line of the email. FDA posts warning letters to www.FDA.gov. Sincerely, /S/ Francis Godwin Director Office of Manufacturing Quality Office of Compliance Center for Drug Evaluation and Research U.S. Food and Drug Administration ______________________ 1 i.e. Quality System, Facilities & Equipment System, Materials System, Production System, Packaging & Labeling System, and Laboratory Control System per FDA’s guidance document Quality Systems Approach to Pharmaceutical CGMP Regulations .
